questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has sudden weakness of her right arm and face and cannot get her words out. Her husband says it began 40 minutes ago while she was gardening. She takes no regular medication. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 152/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG on arrival
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Untreated atrial fibrillation is the main risk factor for ischaemic stroke: thrombus forms in the left atrium and embolises to the cerebral circulation, here the left MCA.

steps.x: Sudden focal deficit with cortical signs, no bleed on CT, and an irregularly irregular pulse.

elim: Usually a younger patient with neck pain or trauma and Horner's syndrome; nothing here suggests it.
CT shows no haemorrhage.
A mimic to exclude with a capillary glucose, but she takes no diabetic medication and the ECG gives a clear embolic source.
Lacunar strokes do not cause dysphasia, a cortical sign.

steps.x: A: Cardioembolism from atrial fibrillation. AF is the main risk factor for ischaemic (cardioembolic) stroke.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man is brought in after his wife found him unable to use his left arm and confused. He had a similar bleed in the right occipital lobe 2 years ago. He has no history of hypertension and takes no anticoagulants. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 132/76 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows a hyperdense haematoma in the right parietal lobe extending to the cortical surface.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of the haemorrhage?
questions.e: Recurrent lobar haemorrhages in an elderly normotensive patient are typical of cerebral amyloid angiopathy; hypertensive bleeds are deep.

clues: right parietal lobe extending to the cortical surface
steps.x: Elderly, normotensive, not anticoagulated, with recurrent lobar (cortical) bleeds.

elim: Usually presents in younger patients; recurrent lobar bleeds in the elderly point to amyloid.
Causes deep bleeds (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons) and he is normotensive.
Needs a preceding ischaemic stroke, usually after thrombolysis.
Causes subarachnoid blood with thunderclap headache, not a lobar parenchymal haematoma.

steps.x: B: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Lobar bleed in the elderly = amyloid angiopathy; deep bleed = hypertension.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has sudden difficulty speaking that began 2 hours ago. His speech is slow, effortful and broken into single words, and he becomes frustrated. He follows the command 'close your eyes and then point to the ceiling' correctly. He also has weakness of his right face and arm. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 164/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
questions.e: Non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension is Broca's (expressive) aphasia from a lesion of the left inferior frontal gyrus.

clues: slow, effortful and broken into single words
steps.x: Expressive problem only: comprehension is intact.

elim: Causes conduction aphasia: fluent speech with inability to repeat.
Wernicke's area: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
Causes slurred (ataxic) speech, not a language deficit.
Language is in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere and his weakness is right-sided, so the lesion is on the left.

steps.x: B: Left inferior frontal gyrus. Broca's aphasia = inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is assessed on the stroke unit. Her speech is fluent, with normal rhythm, and she understands and follows complex instructions. When asked to repeat the phrase 'no ifs, ands or buts' she cannot, and makes many sound substitutions. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging shows a small acute infarct in the left hemisphere. Her BP is 148/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which structure is most likely affected?
questions.e: Fluent speech with intact comprehension but impaired repetition is conduction aphasia, from a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas.

clues: cannot, and makes many sound substitutions
steps.x: Fluent and understands, but cannot repeat.

elim: Broca's area: non-fluent effortful speech.
Causes weakness, not a selective repetition deficit.
Causes hemiballismus.
Wernicke's area: poor comprehension, which she does not have.

steps.x: A: Arcuate fasciculus. Cannot repeat = conduction aphasia = arcuate fasciculus.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man is found by his wife unable to stand. He has weakness of the left face and arm, more than the leg, and ignores people standing on his left side. He denies that anything is wrong. Visual field testing shows a left homonymous hemianopia. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 172/96 mmHg. CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which artery territory is most likely affected?
questions.e: Contralateral face and arm weakness more than the leg, hemianopia and neglect (non-dominant cortical sign) point to the right MCA, which supplies the lateral cortex.

clues: left face and arm, more than the leg
ignores people standing on his left side
steps.x: Left-sided face/arm-predominant weakness with neglect: right lateral cortex.

elim: Causes brainstem signs, quadriplegia or locked-in syndrome.
Would cause right-sided weakness and aphasia.
Weakness would be leg more than arm.
Causes hemianopia with macular sparing but not arm and face weakness or neglect.

steps.x: D: Right middle cerebral artery. Arm > leg with cortical signs = MCA; neglect = non-dominant hemisphere.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had sudden weakness of her right leg since this morning. She can lift her right arm normally, but her right leg is very weak and she has been incontinent of urine twice. Her speech is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 158/90 mmHg and capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: The ACA supplies the medial cortex where the leg is represented, so occlusion gives contralateral leg-predominant weakness with urinary incontinence.

steps.x: Leg more than arm, plus incontinence, on the right.

elim: Weakness would be arm and face more than leg, often with aphasia.
Causes a visual field defect, not leg weakness.
Causes lateral medullary syndrome.
Would cause left leg weakness.

steps.x: A: Left anterior cerebral artery. Leg > arm and incontinence = contralateral ACA.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has sudden difficulty seeing that began 3 hours ago. He keeps missing objects on his left side. He can name a key when it is placed in his hand but cannot recognise it when he looks at it. He has no limb weakness. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 156/88 mmHg. MRI shows an acute right occipital infarct.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on visual field examination?
o: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Left homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing
Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
questions.e: A PCA territory infarct of the occipital cortex causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and may cause visual agnosia.

clues: missing objects on his left side
cannot recognise it when he looks at it
steps.x: Right occipital (PCA) infarct with visual agnosia.

elim: Caused by a chiasmal lesion such as a pituitary tumour.
Typical of an MCA (optic radiation) lesion; occipital PCA infarcts spare the macula.
A right occipital lesion affects the left visual field.
A retinal or optic nerve problem such as amaurosis fugax.

steps.x: B: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. PCA infarct = contralateral hemianopia WITH macular sparing.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has sudden vertigo and is unable to walk. His voice is hoarse and he chokes on sips of water. He has a left-sided ptosis with a small left pupil. Pain and temperature sensation are reduced on the left side of his face and on the right side of his body. Power is normal. His BP is 168/98 mmHg.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg's) syndrome: vertigo, ataxia, dysphagia, ipsilateral Horner's and facial sensory loss with contralateral body pain and temperature loss, from PICA occlusion on the side of the facial signs.

clues: left-sided ptosis with a small left pupil
left side of his face and on the right side of his body
steps.x: Crossed sensory loss, left Horner's, bulbar palsy and vertigo.

elim: Causes locked-in syndrome or bilateral brainstem signs with quadriplegia.
Causes right leg weakness.
Causes a right homonymous hemianopia.
The face and Horner's signs are ipsilateral to the lesion, which is on the left.

steps.x: D: Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Wallenberg's = PICA; the lesion is on the side of the face and Horner's signs.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is found on the floor. He cannot move any of his limbs and cannot speak or move his face. His eyes are open and he blinks and looks up and down when asked, answering questions by blinking. His horizontal eye movements are absent. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 182/100 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: Quadriplegia with bilateral facial and abducens palsy but preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements is locked-in syndrome from acute basilar artery occlusion.

clues: cannot move any of his limbs
blinks and looks up and down
steps.x: Awake, quadriplegic, only vertical eye movements and blinking.

elim: Causes right hemiparesis and aphasia, not quadriplegia with preserved consciousness.
Causes a hemianopia.
Causes lateral medullary syndrome without quadriplegia.
Causes left leg weakness only.

steps.x: A: Basilar artery. Locked-in syndrome = basilar artery occlusion (ventral pons).

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has sudden weakness of her left arm and leg and drooping of her right eyelid. Her right pupil is fixed and dilated and the right eye rests down and out. She has no headache or neck stiffness. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 166/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis is Weber's syndrome, a midbrain infarct from a PCA branch lesion.

clues: right pupil is fixed and dilated
steps.x: Right third nerve palsy with left hemiparesis: a crossed midbrain picture.

elim: Causes crossed sensory loss, Horner's and bulbar signs, not a third nerve palsy with hemiparesis.
Causes quadriplegia with preserved vertical eye movements.
Causes reduced GCS with pinpoint pupils.
Can cause a painful third nerve palsy but not contralateral hemiparesis, and she has no headache.

steps.x: E: Weber's syndrome. Weber's = ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (PCA branch).

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with poorly controlled hypertension collapses at work. Within minutes his GCS is 6. He has no movement in any limb and both pupils are 1 mm. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 214/122 mmHg and respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute. A urine toxicology screen is negative and capillary glucose is 7.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden coma, paralysis and bilateral pinpoint pupils in a hypertensive patient is a pontine haemorrhage, a deep hypertensive bleed.

steps.x: Hypertensive, comatose, quadriplegic, pinpoint pupils, not opioids.

elim: Consciousness is preserved.
Causes pinpoint pupils, but the toxicology is negative and this does not cause hypertension and fever.
Causes a unilateral deficit, not quadriparesis with pinpoint pupils.
Presents with thunderclap headache and meningism, without bilateral pinpoint pupils.

steps.x: C: Pontine haemorrhage. Pinpoint pupils + coma + hypertension = pontine haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension develops sudden, large, uncontrollable flinging movements of her right arm and leg. The movements stop during sleep. She has no weakness, sensory loss or speech disturbance. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 162/90 mmHg and capillary glucose 8.4 mmol/L. MRI shows a small acute lacunar infarct.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the infarct?
questions.e: Unilateral wide-amplitude flinging movements are hemiballismus, caused by a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

clues: large, uncontrollable flinging movements of her right arm and leg
steps.x: Flinging (ballistic) movements on the right.

elim: Causes ipsilateral ataxia and intention tremor, not flinging movements.
Causes pure motor hemiparesis.
Hemiballismus is contralateral to the lesion.
Loss causes parkinsonism with bradykinesia and rest tremor.

steps.x: C: Left subthalamic nucleus. Hemiballismus = contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden weakness of his left face, arm and leg. He cannot see objects to his left, and he does not recognise his own left arm as his. He has atrial fibrillation and stopped his apixaban a month ago. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 158/86 mmHg. CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which is the most likely Oxford (Bamford) classification of this stroke?
questions.e: A TACI needs all three: contralateral hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction (here neglect). Two of three is a PACI.

clues: weakness of his left face, arm and leg
cannot see objects to his left
does not recognise his own left arm
steps.x: Hemiparesis + hemianopia + neglect: all three.

elim: Has no cortical signs or visual field loss.
Needs only two of the three features; he has all three.
Presents with cerebellar or brainstem signs or isolated hemianopia.
Not an Oxford category; posterior strokes are POCS.

steps.x: D: Total anterior circulation infarct. All three features = TACI; two = PACI.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with long-standing hypertension has slurred speech and clumsiness of his right hand that started this morning. He drops his cup but has only mild weakness. Visual fields, language and comprehension are normal and he has no neglect. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular, BP 178/98 mmHg. MRI shows a small deep infarct in the left internal capsule.
questions.q: Which is the most likely Oxford (Bamford) classification of this stroke?
questions.e: Dysarthria with a clumsy hand and no cortical signs is the clumsy-hand dysarthria lacunar syndrome, from a perforating artery infarct of the internal capsule.

clues: slurred speech and clumsiness of his right hand
small deep infarct in the left internal capsule
steps.x: Clumsy hand and dysarthria, no cortical signs, deep small infarct.

elim: Needs a cortical sign or a hemianopia, which he does not have.
Slurred speech here is from the clumsy-hand dysarthria syndrome, without other cerebellar or brainstem signs.
Needs hemiparesis, hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction.
Needs a third nerve palsy.

steps.x: A: Lacunar syndrome. No cortical signs + deep small infarct = lacunar (includes clumsy-hand dysarthria).

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has sudden vertigo, vomiting and difficulty walking. She is unable to walk heel to toe and veers to the right. Her speech is slurred. Power in all four limbs is normal. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 170/94 mmHg. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging shows an acute infarct in the right cerebellar hemisphere.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Posterior circulation (cerebellar) stroke gives DANISH signs ipsilaterally: dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech, hypotonia.

steps.x: Right cerebellar infarct with ataxia and dysarthria.

elim: A lower motor neurone sign seen in motor neurone disease.
Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion, which is on the right.
Suggests functional weakness; her power is normal.
Parkinsonism, not a cerebellar sign.

steps.x: E: Right-sided dysdiadochokinesia. Cerebellar signs (DANISH) are on the same side as the lesion.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man with haemophilia A has a sudden severe headache and weakness of his right arm and leg while lifting weights. He vomits twice. His GCS is 13. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 186/104 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows high-attenuating amorphous material within the left basal ganglia with surrounding oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: High-attenuating (hyperdense) material within the brain parenchyma is intracerebral haemorrhage; haemophilia is a risk factor for haemorrhagic stroke, which is more severe than ischaemic stroke.

clues: high-attenuating amorphous material within the left basal ganglia
steps.x: Bleeding disorder, headache, vomiting and hyperdense material in the brain.

elim: A crescentic collection over the brain surface, usually after trauma.
A ring-enhancing lesion with fever, developing over days.
Early CT is usually normal or shows a hyperdense artery, not high-attenuating material in the brain.
Blood would be in the subarachnoid space and basal cisterns, not within the basal ganglia.

steps.x: C: Haemorrhagic stroke. Hyperdense material within the brain on CT = intracerebral haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman arrives 60 minutes after sudden right-sided weakness and global aphasia. She is assessed with an ABCDE approach and the stroke team is activated. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and irregular, BP 168/92 mmHg and capillary glucose 6.8 mmol/L. An urgent non-contrast CT head is performed before any thrombolysis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Crescent-shaped hyperdense collection crossing suture lines
Hyperdense material in the basal cisterns
questions.e: Early CT in ischaemic stroke is often normal but may show a hyperdense artery sign, here the left MCA (clot in the vessel); the scan is done first to exclude haemorrhage.

clues: 60 minutes after sudden right-sided weakness and global aphasia
steps.x: Hyperacute left MCA stroke, probably embolic from AF.

elim: An acute subdural haemorrhage.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Wrong side, and established hypodensity takes hours to appear.
Abscess or tumour, and this is a non-contrast scan.

steps.x: B: Hyperdense left middle cerebral artery. Hyperdense MCA sign = clot in the artery in ischaemic stroke.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man presents 2 days after sudden numbness of his left hand and face, which has partly improved. He has hypertension and smokes. Examination shows reduced sensation in the left hand only. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 154/90 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head is normal. The team wants to confirm whether he has had an ischaemic infarct.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A normal CT does not exclude ischaemic stroke; diffusion-weighted MRI shows an acute infarct as a bright area and is the test to confirm it.

clues: confirm whether he has had an ischaemic infarct
steps.x: Late, mild, CT normal, need to confirm infarction.

elim: Looks for a source (stenosis) but does not show the infarct.
Adds little; contrast is not used to confirm infarction.
Used for seizures.
Used for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage or infection.

steps.x: E: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging. Confirm an ischaemic infarct with DWI MRI (infarct appears bright).

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has left arm weakness and a right-sided headache with right neck pain that began after a chiropractic neck manipulation yesterday. She has right ptosis and a small right pupil. She has no vascular risk factors. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT angiogram of the head and neck
questions.e: Neck pain and an ipsilateral Horner's after neck manipulation with a contralateral deficit suggests carotid artery dissection, investigated with CT angiography of the head and neck.

clues: right ptosis and a small right pupil
steps.x: Young, neck trauma, neck pain, Horner's and a stroke.

elim: Looks for a patent foramen ovale; the neck pain and Horner's here point to dissection.
Used for seizures.
Used for subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT after 6 hours.
Considered in young strokes with no cause; here there is an obvious cause to confirm.

steps.x: B: CT angiogram of the head and neck. Suspected carotid dissection = CT head and neck angiogram.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man is on the stroke rehabilitation ward 3 weeks after a left MCA infarct. The occupational therapist wants to record how independent he is with feeding, washing, dressing, using the toilet, transfers and walking, and to repeat the score before discharge to plan his care package.
questions.q: Which assessment tool is most appropriate?
questions.e: The Barthel Index measures functional independence in activities of daily living after stroke.

clues: feeding, washing, dressing, using the toilet, transfers and walking
steps.x: The question is about activities of daily living.

elim: Predicts 3-month outcome after alteplase.
Predicts short-term mortality after ischaemic stroke.
Measures neurological severity at presentation, not daily living.
Used in the emergency department to recognise stroke.

steps.x: A: Barthel Index. ADL disability after stroke = Barthel Index.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman was given IV alteplase 2 hours after onset of a left MCA stroke. Two days later her family ask how likely she is to be independent in 3 months. The consultant uses a score that includes the hyperdense artery sign on CT, pre-stroke disability, age, glucose, onset-to-treatment time and NIH Stroke Scale score.
questions.q: Which score is being used?
questions.e: The DRAGON score predicts 3-month prognosis after thrombolysis with alteplase; the modified SOAR score predicts short-term mortality.

steps.x: Prognosis at 3 months after alteplase.

elim: Records current ADL function, not a prediction after thrombolysis.
Measures conscious level.
Predicts short-term mortality after ischaemic stroke (0 to 9), not 3-month outcome after alteplase.
Recognises stroke in the emergency department.

steps.x: B: DRAGON score. DRAGON = 3-month outcome after alteplase; SOAR = short-term mortality.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is brought in by ambulance with sudden right arm weakness and slurred speech. The triage nurse checks for loss of consciousness, seizure activity, facial, arm and leg weakness, speech disturbance and visual field defect, to decide quickly whether this is a stroke rather than a mimic such as hypoglycaemia or migraine.
questions.q: Which tool is the nurse using?
questions.e: The ROSIER scale is used in the emergency department to recognise stroke and separate it from mimics; loss of consciousness and seizure score negatively.

steps.x: Emergency department, recognising stroke versus mimic.

elim: Measures ADL independence after stroke.
Estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.
Predicts outcome after alteplase.
Grades disability, not stroke recognition.

steps.x: E: ROSIER scale. Recognising stroke in ED = ROSIER.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman says she cannot move her right leg after an argument. She has no headache. Reflexes and plantar responses are normal. When she lies supine and is asked to flex her left hip against resistance, the examiner feels strong downward pressure from the right heel, although she cannot push the right leg down when asked directly. Her BP is 122/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which examination finding is being demonstrated?
questions.e: Hoover's sign separates organic from functional leg weakness: involuntary hip extension of the 'weak' leg appears when the other hip flexes against resistance.

clues: flex her left hip against resistance
strong downward pressure from the right heel
Reflexes and plantar responses are normal
steps.x: Weak leg pushes down involuntarily when the other hip flexes.

elim: An upgoing plantar from an upper motor neurone lesion; her plantars are normal.
Shows proprioceptive loss.
A sign of organic upper motor neurone weakness of the arm.
An upper motor neurone sign; her reflexes are normal.

steps.x: B: Positive Hoover's sign. Hoover's sign = functional (non-organic) leg weakness.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide is found by a carer to be drowsy, sweaty and weak down his left side. His GCS is 13 and he has left arm and leg weakness. His pulse rate is 102 bpm, BP 144/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The paramedic is about to transfer him to the stroke unit.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Hypoglycaemia can cause focal deficits that mimic stroke; check capillary glucose first, especially in a patient on a sulfonylurea.

steps.x: On a sulfonylurea, sweaty, drowsy, focal deficit.

elim: Part of later work-up for a source, not initial.
Not first; a reversible mimic must be excluded at the bedside.
Needed urgently, but hypoglycaemia must be checked first in seconds at the bedside.
Hyponatraemia is a mimic, but a capillary glucose is quicker and more likely given gliclazide.

steps.x: A: Capillary blood glucose. Every suspected stroke: check capillary glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has an ischaemic stroke confirmed on MRI. She has had three miscarriages and a deep vein thrombosis last year. She does not smoke and has no hypertension, diabetes or family history. ECG shows sinus rhythm, carotid Doppler is normal and a bubble echocardiogram shows no shunt.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT angiogram of the head and neck
questions.e: Under 55 with no obvious cause, screen for thrombophilia and autoimmune disease; recurrent miscarriage plus venous and arterial thrombosis suggests antiphospholipid syndrome.

steps.x: Young, no vascular risk factors, recurrent miscarriage and thrombosis.

elim: For phaeochromocytoma, not suggested here.
Looks for dissection, which has no clue here.
Used for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage or infection.
Already negative; a repeat adds nothing.

steps.x: E: Thrombophilia and autoimmune screen. Young stroke, no cause: thrombophilia (including antiphospholipid) and autoimmune screen.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man attends his GP surgery with his wife. Thirty minutes ago he developed sudden weakness of his left arm and drooping of the left side of his face, which are still present. His wife offers to drive him straight to the emergency department. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 176/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial action?
o: Advise his wife to drive him to the emergency department
Give aspirin 300 mg and refer to the TIA clinic
Lower his BP with oral amlodipine
Request an urgent outpatient CT head
questions.e: Ongoing stroke symptoms in a GP setting need a 999 emergency ambulance to a hyperacute stroke unit; aspirin is not given before a bleed is excluded.

steps.x: Ongoing deficit within the thrombolysis window, in primary care.

elim: Delays treatment and gives no care if he deteriorates; an ambulance pre-alerts the stroke team.
This is for a resolved TIA; his symptoms are ongoing and he may need thrombolysis.
BP is not lowered in the community before imaging.
Far too slow for a possible thrombolysis candidate.

steps.x: B: Call 999 for an emergency ambulance. Stroke in the GP surgery: call 999.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has sudden right arm weakness and expressive dysphasia that started 2 hours ago. Her NIH Stroke Scale score is 8. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 164/88 mmHg and capillary glucose 7.2 mmol/L. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. CT angiogram shows no large vessel occlusion. She has no contraindications to treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours, haemorrhage excluded and BP below 185/110 mmHg: give IV thrombolysis with alteplase (or tenecteplase).

steps.x: Within 4.5 hours, no bleed, BP acceptable, no large vessel occlusion.

elim: Given if not thrombolysed; she is within 4.5 hours so should be thrombolysed.
Secondary prevention, started at 14 days.
For malignant MCA oedema, not a moderate stroke at 2 hours.
Needs a large artery occlusion, which she does not have.

steps.x: D: IV alteplase. Ischaemic stroke under 4.5 hours with no bleed: IV alteplase.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has had left arm and leg weakness for 90 minutes. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. He is a candidate for thrombolysis but his BP is 198/112 mmHg on two readings. The registrar starts IV labetalol and plans to give alteplase once the target is reached. His pulse rate is 88 bpm.
questions.q: Below which BP must his blood pressure be before thrombolysis?
questions.e: BP must be reduced below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis to reduce the risk of haemorrhage.

steps.x: He needs thrombolysis but his BP is too high.

elim: Far too low; over-lowering BP risks extending the infarct.
The systolic target of below 140 mmHg is used in intracerebral haemorrhage, not before thrombolysis.
Not the thrombolysis threshold.
Used when deciding whether to lower BP in strokes not being thrombolysed.

steps.x: D: 185/110 mmHg. Before alteplase, BP below 185/110 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman woke at 07:00 with right-sided weakness and dysphasia. She was last seen well at 23:00 the night before, 8 hours earlier. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage and CT angiogram shows no large vessel occlusion. CT perfusion shows a small infarct core with a large area of salvageable tissue. Her BP is 162/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Observe and repeat CT in 24 hours
questions.e: Thrombolysis can be extended to 9 hours from onset (or the midpoint of sleep) when CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI shows salvageable tissue.

steps.x: Wake-up stroke beyond 4.5 hours but with salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging.

elim: Ignores the imaging, which shows salvageable tissue within the extended window.
For malignant MCA infarction with reduced consciousness.
Needs a large artery occlusion.
Misses the chance to save the penumbra.

steps.x: C: IV thrombolysis. Extended thrombolysis window 0 to 9 hours if imaging shows salvageable tissue.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man presents 14 hours after sudden onset of right arm weakness and dysarthria that are improving. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. CT angiogram shows no large vessel occlusion and no perfusion imaging is available. He has passed a bedside swallow screen. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular and BP 166/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: An ischaemic stroke not being thrombolysed needs aspirin 300 mg within 24 hours (rectally or by tube if the swallow is unsafe), continued for 2 weeks.

steps.x: Too late for lysis, no occlusion for thrombectomy, bleed excluded.

elim: He is in sinus rhythm; anticoagulation is not indicated.
Long-term secondary prevention from 14 days.
He is outside the thrombolysis window with no imaging of salvageable tissue.
No large vessel occlusion.

steps.x: B: Aspirin 300 mg. Not thrombolysed: aspirin 300 mg within 24 hours (after 24 hours if thrombolysed).

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has sudden left hemiparesis, left hemianopia and neglect that began 2 hours ago. His NIH Stroke Scale score is 18. Non-contrast CT head shows no haemorrhage. CT angiogram shows occlusion of the proximal right middle cerebral artery. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 170/96 mmHg. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Within 4.5 hours with a proximal MCA or ICA occlusion, combine IV thrombolysis with mechanical thrombectomy (within 6 hours).

clues: occlusion of the proximal right middle cerebral artery
steps.x: Large artery occlusion, within 4.5 hours.

elim: He is eligible for reperfusion therapy.
For malignant oedema with reduced consciousness, not first-line.
With a proximal large artery occlusion, thrombectomy should be added.
He is within 4.5 hours, so thrombolysis should be given as well.

steps.x: D: IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy. Large artery occlusion under 4.5 hours: thrombolysis plus thrombectomy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman was last seen well 12 hours ago and now has right hemiparesis and global aphasia. Before this she lived independently (modified Rankin score 1). Her NIH Stroke Scale score is 17. CT angiogram shows occlusion of the left internal carotid artery terminus and CT perfusion shows a small core with a large area of salvageable tissue. Her BP is 158/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Thrombectomy can be offered 6 to 24 hours after onset for a large artery occlusion with salvageable tissue; it benefits most patients with pre-stroke modified Rankin score below 3 and NIHSS above 5.

steps.x: Large artery occlusion at 12 hours, salvageable tissue, good baseline, severe deficit.

elim: Misses an effective reperfusion treatment within 24 hours.
Used for secondary prevention of carotid stenosis, not acute occlusion.
She is beyond the thrombolysis windows; thrombectomy is the option for a large artery occlusion.
Not used to treat acute ischaemic stroke.

steps.x: E: Mechanical thrombectomy. Thrombectomy extended window 6 to 24 hours with salvageable tissue.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man had a right MCA infarct yesterday. Today he is drowsy with a GCS of 11, worsening from 15. His pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 184/96 mmHg. Repeat CT head shows infarction of more than 50% of the right MCA territory with swelling and midline shift. There is no haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Malignant MCA infarction (under 60, severe stroke, falling consciousness, infarct of at least 50% of the MCA territory) needs decompressive hemicraniectomy to relieve raised ICP and prevent herniation.

clues: more than 50% of the right MCA territory
steps.x: Young, falling GCS, large MCA infarct with swelling.

elim: Too late, and will not help oedema.
Dangerous with a mass lesion and midline shift.
Does not treat established infarction with oedema.
Used to prevent vasospasm in subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: A: Decompressive hemicraniectomy. Malignant MCA oedema under 60: decompressive hemicraniectomy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman had an ischaemic stroke 14 days ago and has been taking aspirin 300 mg daily. She had a severe rash with clopidogrel in the past. ECG and 24 hour tape show sinus rhythm throughout. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. Her total cholesterol is 5.9 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term secondary prevention?
o: Aspirin 75 mg daily plus atorvastatin 80 mg at night
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily plus atorvastatin 20 mg at night
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily plus atorvastatin 80 mg at night
questions.e: From 14 days after ischaemic stroke, give clopidogrel 75 mg daily, or aspirin 75 mg if clopidogrel is contraindicated, plus atorvastatin 80 mg at night.

steps.x: Two weeks after stroke, cannot take clopidogrel, not in AF.

elim: Only for AF-associated stroke; she is in sinus rhythm.
300 mg is the acute dose for 2 weeks; the long-term dose is 75 mg.
Contraindicated drug and the wrong statin dose.
First choice, but she is allergic to clopidogrel.

steps.x: C: Aspirin 75 mg daily plus atorvastatin 80 mg at night. Secondary prevention: clopidogrel 75 mg (aspirin 75 mg if not tolerated) + atorvastatin 80 mg.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has a moderate left MCA ischaemic stroke and is found to have new atrial fibrillation. He was not thrombolysed and is taking aspirin 300 mg daily. MRI shows a medium-sized infarct without haemorrhage. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and irregular, BP 148/84 mmHg. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5.
questions.q: When is it most appropriate to start anticoagulation?
questions.e: In AF-associated ischaemic stroke, start anticoagulation (for example apixaban 5 mg twice daily) 2 weeks after the event; after a TIA it starts immediately once haemorrhage is excluded.

steps.x: Established infarct with AF.

elim: Too early after a moderate stroke; risk of haemorrhagic transformation.
Too late; leaves him without stroke prevention.
This applies after a TIA, not an established infarct.
Aspirin does not adequately prevent cardioembolic stroke in AF.

steps.x: A: 2 weeks after the stroke. AF stroke: anticoagulate at 2 weeks; TIA: anticoagulate immediately.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation develops sudden left-sided weakness and headache. Her GCS is 14. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and irregular and BP 150/88 mmHg. Non-contrast CT head shows a right thalamic intracerebral haemorrhage. Her last dose of dabigatran was 3 hours ago.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment to reverse her anticoagulation?
o: IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
questions.e: Intracerebral haemorrhage on dabigatran needs urgent reversal with idarucizumab before any neurosurgery; warfarin is reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K.

steps.x: Haemorrhagic stroke on a direct thrombin inhibitor.

elim: Reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban, not dabigatran.
Does not reliably reverse direct thrombin inhibitors.
Used for warfarin reversal.
Reverses heparin.

steps.x: C: Idarucizumab. Dabigatran reversal = idarucizumab.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a left basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage confirmed on CT 40 minutes ago. He is not anticoagulated. His GCS is 14 and he is protecting his airway. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 196/104 mmHg. The neurosurgical team advise medical management and he is admitted for monitoring.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood pressure target?
o: No BP lowering for the first 24 hours
Systolic BP below 100 mmHg within 1 hour
Systolic BP below 140 mmHg within 1 hour
Systolic BP below 160 mmHg within 24 hours
questions.e: In acute intracerebral haemorrhage, lower systolic BP to below 140 mmHg (ideally not below 120 mmHg) within 1 hour, for example with IV labetalol or GTN.

steps.x: Acute haemorrhagic stroke with high BP.

elim: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in haemorrhage.
Raised BP drives haematoma expansion and should be lowered.
Too low; the lower limit is about 110 to 120 mmHg.
Too slow and too high a target.

steps.x: D: Systolic BP below 140 mmHg within 1 hour. ICH: systolic below 140 mmHg within 1 hour.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman was admitted with a left MCA infarct yesterday. During a bedside swallow screen with water she coughs, her voice becomes wet and gurgly, and she drools from the right side of her mouth. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 150/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Insert a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy now
Keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids and request a speech and language therapy assessment
Start IV antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia
Thicken fluids and continue oral medicines
questions.e: An unsafe swallow (coughing, wet voice, drooling) after stroke means nil by mouth with IV fluids and a SALT assessment, to prevent aspiration pneumonia.

clues: coughs, her voice becomes wet and gurgly
steps.x: Failed swallow screen after a stroke.

elim: An unsafe swallow risks aspiration.
Too early; a PEG is for long-term failure after SALT assessment.
She has no signs of infection.
Diet changes are decided by SALT after assessment.

steps.x: C: Keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids and request a speech and language therapy assessment. Unsafe swallow: NBM, IV fluids, SALT.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man received IV alteplase for a right MCA stroke. Twenty-six hours later he was started on aspirin 300 mg. On day 3 he develops a headache and becomes drowsy with worsening left arm weakness. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 192/100 mmHg. Repeat CT head shows new hyperdense blood within the area of infarction.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Give a second dose of IV alteplase
Stop aspirin and control blood pressure
questions.e: Haemorrhagic transformation is a recognised complication after thrombolysis, from reperfusion into necrotic, leaky tissue; stop aspirin 300 mg and control BP.

clues: new hyperdense blood within the area of infarction
steps.x: Bleeding into an infarct after thrombolysis and antiplatelets.

elim: Would worsen the bleed.
Antiplatelets worsen haemorrhagic transformation.
There is no new occlusion; this is a bleed.
Anticoagulation is contraindicated with active bleeding.

steps.x: E: Stop aspirin and control blood pressure. Haemorrhagic transformation: stop aspirin, control BP.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has sudden left arm weakness and dysarthria on the day after a 14 hour flight. Her right calf is swollen and tender. She has no vascular risk factors. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and regular, BP 124/76 mmHg. MRI confirms a right MCA territory infarct. A bubble echocardiogram shows microbubbles crossing into the left atrium.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her stroke?
o: Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Rupture of a carotid atherosclerotic plaque
questions.e: A venous clot from the leg crossed to the arterial side through a patent foramen ovale (shown by bubbles crossing on echocardiography) and embolised to the brain.

clues: right calf is swollen and tender
microbubbles crossing into the left atrium
steps.x: Young, DVT, right-to-left shunt on bubble echo.

elim: Her pulse is regular.
No neck pain, trauma or Horner's.
Unlikely at 26 with no risk factors.
A hypertensive lacunar mechanism; she is young and normotensive.

steps.x: C: Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale. Young stroke + DVT + bubbles crossing = paradoxical embolism via PFO.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a left MCA occlusion 90 minutes after onset. CT perfusion shows a small central area with no blood flow surrounded by a much larger area with reduced flow but preserved tissue. The consultant explains to his wife why thrombolysis and thrombectomy must be given as quickly as possible. His BP is 168/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the main aim of these reperfusion treatments?
o: Dissolve the infarcted core so it recovers
Restore flow to hypoperfused tissue before it infarcts
questions.e: The ischaemic penumbra is hypoperfused but not yet infarcted; it is the target of hyperacute reperfusion and shrinks with time, so 'time is brain'.

clues: small central area with no blood flow
steps.x: A core and a much larger penumbra.

elim: Infarcted tissue is dead and cannot recover.
That is the aim of decompressive surgery.
Reperfusion does not treat the embolic source.
Vasospasm is a complication of subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: D: Restore flow to hypoperfused tissue before it infarcts. Reperfusion targets the penumbra, which is lost with every minute.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with untreated hypertension for 15 years has sudden right hemiparesis and sensory loss. He is not anticoagulated and has no history of trauma. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 210/118 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping. Non-contrast CT head shows a hyperdense haematoma in the left thalamus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the haemorrhage?
o: Amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls
Bleeding into a primary brain tumour
Rupture of small penetrating arteries weakened by chronic hypertension
questions.e: Chronic hypertensive vasculopathy weakens small penetrating arteries, which rupture into deep structures: basal ganglia, thalamus and pons. Hypertension is the strongest overall stroke risk factor.

steps.x: Long-standing hypertension and a deep bleed.

elim: Causes lobar bleeds in the elderly, not deep thalamic bleeds.
No preceding history of headache or progressive symptoms.
Haemorrhagic transformation follows an ischaemic stroke, often after thrombolysis.
Bleeds into the subarachnoid space.

steps.x: E: Rupture of small penetrating arteries weakened by chronic hypertension. Deep bleed (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons) = hypertensive vasculopathy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has sudden weakness of the right side of her face and right arm, with only mild weakness of the right leg. She has word-finding difficulty. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 160/90 mmHg. CT angiogram shows occlusion of a branch of the left middle cerebral artery. A medical student asks why her arm is so much weaker than her leg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: The ACA supplies the lateral cortex where the arm is represented
The arm has more lower motor neurones affected
The leg is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery
The leg motor tracts cross in the medulla but the arm tracts do not
The MCA supplies the lateral cortex where the face and arm are represented
questions.e: The deficit reflects the territory affected: the MCA supplies the lateral cortex (face, arm and language areas), the ACA the medial cortex (leg).

clues: right side of her face and right arm
only mild weakness of the right leg
steps.x: Face and arm more than leg with aphasia.

elim: The ACA supplies the medial cortex, where the leg is represented.
This is an upper motor neurone lesion of the cortex.
The PCA supplies the occipital cortex and visual areas.
Both arm and leg corticospinal fibres decussate in the medulla.

steps.x: E: The MCA supplies the lateral cortex where the face and arm are represented. Lateral cortex (MCA) = face, arm, language; medial cortex (ACA) = leg.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had a large left MCA infarct 2 days ago. He becomes increasingly drowsy and his right pupil now reacts normally but his left pupil is dilated and sluggish. His pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 196/104 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute. CT head shows swelling of the infarcted hemisphere with midline shift and no new haemorrhage.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his deterioration?
o: Cerebral oedema raising intracranial pressure and causing herniation
Recurrent embolism to the right MCA
questions.e: Oedema in a large infarct raises ICP and causes secondary injury by herniation (Cushing's response, third nerve compression); this is why decompressive surgery is used in malignant MCA infarction.

clues: left pupil is dilated and sluggish
pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 196/104 mmHg
swelling of the infarcted hemisphere with midline shift
steps.x: Day 2 of a large infarct, falling GCS, blown pupil and Cushing's response.

elim: A delayed complication of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
CT shows no new haemorrhage.
Would not cause a unilateral dilated pupil and midline shift.
Would cause new left-sided signs, not a dilated left pupil with midline shift.

steps.x: A: Cerebral oedema raising intracranial pressure and causing herniation. Malignant oedema raises ICP and causes herniation.
